summary.text: A galaxy is a physical system of stars, planetary systems, stellar remnants, gas, dust and dark matter bound together by gravity.
Galaxies are categorised by their visual characteristics as elliptical, spiral or irregular, and the Milky Way is a spiral.
Most galaxies are gravitationally organised into groups, clusters and superclusters, arranged into sheets and filaments around immense voids.

facts.label: Galaxy count
facts.value: Between 200 billion and 2 trillion in the observable universe

facts.label: Dark matter
facts.value: Holds most of a typical galaxy's mass

items.prompt: If you could weigh a typical galaxy, where would most of its mass turn out to be?

options.label: In dark matter, with stars and nebulae a small share
In the stars you can see
In the gas and dust between the stars
In the black hole at its center

items.explain: Most of the mass in a typical galaxy is dark matter, with only a few percent visible as stars and nebulae.

items.prompt: Messier 109 is also called NGC 3992 and UGC 6937. Why does one galaxy have so many names?

options.label: It was rediscovered and renamed several times
Each name marks a different part of the galaxy
Each catalogue gives the same galaxy its own number
The numbers show how far away it is

items.explain: All the well-known galaxies appear in one or more catalogues, each time under a different number.

items.prompt: Kapteyn and Shapley drew very different pictures of the Milky Way. What did both analyses overlook?

options.label: The gravity of other galaxies pulling on its stars
Dust in the galactic plane that absorbs starlight
Stars hidden behind the Sun's own glare
Changes in the Sun's brightness over time

items.explain: Both failed to account for light absorption by interstellar dust until Trumpler quantified it in 1930.

items.prompt: Zooming out from the Milky Way, which description of its surroundings is right?

options.label: It sits in the Local Group, which is part of the Virgo Supercluster
It sits in the Virgo Supercluster, which is part of the Local Group
It floats alone in a void with no other galaxies near
It sits in a group made only of Milky Way-sized galaxies

items.explain: The Milky Way is part of the Local Group, which is part of the Virgo Supercluster.

items.prompt: Astronomers can model a star forming from a dense gas cloud well. How well is the formation of a whole galaxy understood?

options.label: Fully, by the same models that explain single stars
Better than star formation, since galaxies are larger
Well, since it takes only a few thousand years
Less well, and it plays out over about a billion years

items.explain: Star formation has good models, but galaxy formation is less well understood and operates on a scale of a billion years.

items.prompt: If galaxies were coins scattered across a huge table, how would the gaps compare with the coins' own sizes?

options.label: The gaps would be many times wider than the coins
The coins would touch or overlap constantly
The gaps would roughly equal the coins' widths
The gaps would be thinner than a single coin

beats.title: Islands of stars in the dark
beats.hook: At least 200 billion galaxies fill the observable universe, yet astronomers once could not say what these objects even were.

beats.prompt: A faint smudge on the sky is resolved by a big telescope into countless stars, but each star looks very faint. What do astronomers conclude?
beats.explain: Larger telescopes resolved a few nearby bright galaxies into huge conglomerations of stars, and their apparent faintness and star numbers put them well beyond the Milky Way, so they were called island universes.

choices.label: It is a small star cluster inside the Milky Way
choices.feedback: A cluster nearby is a natural guess, but the faintness and sheer number of stars place such objects well beyond the Milky Way.

choices.label: It is a glowing gas cloud with no stars
choices.feedback: Early observers thought of them as nebulae, but larger telescopes resolved them into huge conglomerations of stars.

choices.label: It lies far beyond the Milky Way

beats.explain: A galaxy holds stars, gas, dust and dark matter bound by gravity, while groups and superclusters are made up of many galaxies.

beats.prompt: put these steps in our picture of the Milky Way in order

items.label: Galileo sees that the Milky Way is made of many faint stars (1610)
Thomas Wright guesses it is a rotating body of stars (1750)
Kant builds on Wright's idea in a treatise (1755)
William Herschel counts stars to map its shape (1785)

beats.explain: The dates run 1610, 1750, 1755 and 1785, each step building toward a picture of the Milky Way's structure.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about Andromeda is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The Milky Way is at least 26,800 parsecs across.
Its nearest large neighbour, Andromeda, is just over 750,000 parsecs away.
That distance is many times the Milky Way's own width.
So Andromeda must be a part of the Milky Way itself.

beats.explain: At that distance Andromeda is a separate galaxy: galaxies are separated by distances far larger than their own sizes.

beats.idea: A galaxy is a gravity-bound system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, and the Milky Way is only one among vast numbers of them.

paragraphs.heading: What a galaxy is
paragraphs.text: A galaxy is a system of stars, planetary systems, the remains of stars, gas, dust and dark matter, all held together by gravity. The name comes from a Greek word meaning milky, a nod to the Milky Way, the galaxy that holds our Solar System. Most of a typical galaxy's mass is dark matter, and stars and nebulae make up only a few percent of it. Supermassive black holes are a common feature at galactic centers.

paragraphs.heading: Sizes and numbers
paragraphs.text: Galaxies hold about 100 million stars on average, but they range from dwarfs with under a thousand stars to supergiants with one hundred trillion. Each of those stars orbits its galaxy's center of mass. Most galaxies are 1,000 to 100,000 parsecs across, roughly 3,000 to 300,000 light years. The Milky Way is at least 26,800 parsecs wide, and Andromeda, its nearest large neighbour, lies just over 750,000 parsecs away. Estimates put the count in the observable universe between 200 billion and 2 trillion.

paragraphs.heading: Shapes and groups
paragraphs.text: Astronomers sort galaxies by how they look: elliptical, spiral or irregular. The Milky Way is a spiral. Some galaxies stand out for other reasons, such as interacting with another galaxy, forming stars at an unusual pace, or hosting an active galactic nucleus. Most galaxies are bound by gravity into groups, clusters and superclusters; ours belongs to the Local Group, which it dominates together with Andromeda, inside the Virgo Supercluster. On the largest scale, these gatherings form sheets and filaments around immense voids.

paragraphs.heading: Island universes
paragraphs.text: Galaxies were first spotted through telescopes and called spiral nebulae. Most astronomers of the 18th and 19th centuries saw them as unresolved star clusters or as extragalactic nebulae, and what they really were stayed a mystery. Larger telescopes later broke a few bright nearby ones, such as Andromeda, into vast crowds of stars, and their faintness placed them far beyond the Milky Way. People began calling them island universes. Harlow Shapley pushed for the word galaxy, but the influential Edwin Hubble kept saying nebulae, and the naming did not fully change until after Hubble died in 1953.

paragraphs.heading: Mapping our own galaxy
paragraphs.text: The Greek philosopher Democritus suggested that the bright band of the Milky Way might be made of distant stars. Galileo gave proof in 1610, when his telescope showed it held a huge number of faint stars. In 1750 Thomas Wright guessed it was a rotating body of stars bound by gravity, seen as a band because we look out from inside its disk. Later, Kapteyn and Harlow Shapley drew very different maps: one put the Sun near the center of a small galaxy, the other far from the center of a wide flat disk. Both ignored how dust dims light, and the modern picture came only after Robert Julius Trumpler measured that effect in 1930.

paragraphs.heading: Naming them
paragraphs.text: Millions of galaxies have been catalogued, but only a handful have well-known names, like Andromeda, the Magellanic Clouds, the Whirlpool and the Sombrero. Astronomers work with numbers from catalogues such as Messier's and the NGC, and each well-known galaxy carries a different number in every catalogue that lists it. The spiral Messier 109, for example, is also NGC 3992 and UGC 6937. A few galaxies beyond our own can be seen on a dark night with the unaided eye, including Andromeda, both Magellanic Clouds and the Triangulum Galaxy.
